items.prompt: An external application sends events to an ingestion API and only registered tenants may publish. Which front-door controls should be combined?
constraints: Publish rate and abuse must be controlled.

options.text: Use API authentication and authorization, request validation, WAF or abuse controls where appropriate, usage plans or throttling, and a durable downstream ingestion contract.
Treat the event name as the tenant credential.
Allow anonymous writes and identify tenants only in the payload.
Put the API behind a private subnet and remove application authorization.

feedback.Reason: A public ingestion endpoint needs identity, authorization, validation, and rate controls before events enter the data path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: API Gateway and WAF provide front-door controls while Kinesis, Firehose, or a queue provides durable downstream buffering.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates tenant identity, schema, size, quota, retry, and failure responses and records rejected requests.
Details.errorCorrection: Authentication alone does not guarantee the tenant can publish to the requested resource.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strong front-door controls add latency and configuration but reduce abuse and malformed data.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A public or guessable name is not authentication.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Payload identity cannot prevent unauthorized writes or spoofing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network placement does not replace caller identity and tenant authorization.

items.prompt: Private workloads in several VPCs must publish to a regional AWS ingestion service without traversing the public internet. What network pattern should be evaluated?
constraints: The service supports a VPC endpoint or private path.
DNS and endpoint policies are controlled.

options.text: Use the supported interface or gateway endpoint pattern, restrict endpoint policies and security groups, and verify private DNS, routing, and service authorization.
Send all traffic through an internet gateway and rely on TLS alone.
Create a public DNS alias and call it private.
Allow every principal to use the endpoint for convenience.

feedback.Reason: Private connectivity is a combined route, endpoint, DNS, and policy design.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS PrivateLink and VPC endpoints provide service-specific private access with endpoint policies and security controls.
Details.scenarioApplication: The network team tests resolution and route from each VPC and confirms denied access to unrelated streams or destinations.
Details.errorCorrection: Not every service or API operation supports the same endpoint type and behavior.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Private endpoints reduce egress exposure but add endpoint, DNS, and multi-VPC management cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: TLS protects transport but does not meet the stated private path requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS naming does not change the network route or exposure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Endpoint access still needs identity and resource scoping.

items.prompt: A Kinesis Data Streams workload reaches write throttling during predictable traffic growth, and per-key ordering is required. What should be evaluated?
constraints: Traffic volume grows by partition key.

options.text: Model partition-key distribution, increase or reshard capacity as appropriate, spread hot keys without breaking ordering, and alert before retention threatens recovery.
Use one constant partition key to make all records globally ordered.
Choose random keys and ignore per-device ordering.
Retry throttled writes without backoff or capacity change.

feedback.Reason: Shard capacity must be matched to both aggregate rate and the hot-key distribution.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis partitions provide throughput and ordering boundaries based on partition keys.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures records, bytes, hot keys, retries, and consumer lag and tests a key-sharding strategy before production growth.
Details.errorCorrection: Resharding can change cost and operational behavior and cannot repair a fundamentally unbalanced business key alone.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More partitions improve parallelism but require consumer and downstream scaling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A constant key concentrates writes and limits throughput.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Random distribution can break the required ordering scope.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unbounded retry amplifies pressure and does not add service capacity.

items.prompt: A Firehose delivery stream sends data to S3, and the owner accepts up to five-minute freshness to reduce tiny objects. What should be configured?
constraints: Object size and downstream scan efficiency matter.

options.text: Tune Firehose buffering by time and size within the freshness objective, then monitor delivery lag, object size, failures, and downstream partition layout.
Set the buffer to one second regardless of the freshness and file-size goal.
Buffer forever until the largest possible object is reached.
Disable destination failure monitoring because Firehose retries internally.

feedback.Reason: Buffering is a latency, object-size, and failure-recovery tradeoff.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Firehose buffers records by configured size or time before delivery and exposes delivery and error behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests burst and idle workloads, verifies destination object layout, and alerts before buffer age exceeds the SLO.
Details.errorCorrection: The chosen buffer cannot exceed the business freshness boundary or downstream recovery window.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Larger buffers improve file efficiency but delay visibility and can increase loss scope during failure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Very short buffering can produce small objects and higher downstream overhead.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unbounded buffering violates the freshness objective and hides delivery failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Managed retries do not remove the need to observe persistent failure and lag.

items.prompt: Firehose needs a lightweight record transformation before S3 delivery, but transformation failures must not silently discard records. What design is required?
constraints: Raw or failed records need recovery.

options.text: Use the supported Firehose transformation path with bounded function capacity, preserve or route failed records, and monitor processing and delivery failures separately.
Drop records when the transform times out so delivery stays fast.
Run an unbounded multi-hour ETL job inside the per-record transform.
Assume destination success means transformation success for every record.

feedback.Reason: Inline transformation needs its own timeout, retry, error, and record-preservation contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Firehose can invoke supported transformations before destination delivery and reports processing and delivery failures.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests malformed records, timeout, retry, error output, and idempotent transformation behavior under burst load.
Details.errorCorrection: Complex enrichment or backfill should move to a separate durable processing stage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Inline transformation is convenient but couples delivery throughput to function capacity and failure behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Silent loss violates the delivery contract and hides the cause.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The transformation hook needs bounded execution and is not a general batch engine.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A destination can receive a partial result while records are rejected or retried.

items.prompt: An MSK cluster experiences broker disk growth and consumer lag while producers remain within average throughput. What capacity dimensions should be reviewed?
constraints: Consumers and brokers have separate bottlenecks.

options.text: Review broker storage, network, partition count and distribution, retention, replication, consumer lag, and burst headroom before changing instance size or adding brokers.
Add producers because more input will clear consumer lag.
Delete old topics immediately without checking retention and replay needs.
Scale only CPU because disk and network never affect Kafka throughput.

feedback.Reason: MSK capacity is multidimensional and must be chosen from measured broker and consumer signals.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kafka brokers distribute partition leaders and replicas across storage, network, and compute resources.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator correlates disk, network, CPU, partition skew, replication, and lag and tests a capacity change with a replay plan.
Details.errorCorrection: More brokers do not automatically rebalance every hotspot and can add partition movement cost.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Capacity headroom protects bursts but increases steady-state cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More input increases backlog and cannot solve a broker or consumer bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unplanned deletion can remove recovery evidence and violate retention.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Kafka performance depends on storage, network, partition, and replication behavior as well as CPU.

items.prompt: Two applications read the same MSK topic: one needs every event and another needs a competing work queue. How should consumer groups be assigned?

options.text: Use distinct consumer groups for independent full-topic processing and the appropriate shared group for work distribution, with retention and replay policies per application.
Put both applications in one group so every application receives every record.
Use one global offset for all applications.
Delete records after the first application reads them.

feedback.Reason: Consumer-group semantics determine whether records are broadcast by group or distributed within a group.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kafka consumer groups maintain independent offsets and assign partitions among members of the same group.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect models replay, lag, partition count, and retention for each application and tests a stopped consumer.
Details.errorCorrection: A group cannot provide more parallelism than its assigned partitions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Independent groups improve isolation but multiply read and retention cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A consumer group distributes records among members rather than broadcasting to each member.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Independent recovery and replay needs require separate offset state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Kafka retention and group offsets support multiple consumers without immediate deletion.

items.prompt: A consumer cannot parse some records, and repeated retries block later records in the same processing path. What recovery pattern is appropriate?
constraints: The original payload is needed for correction.

options.text: Use bounded retries with durable error or dead-letter storage, preserve the original record and failure reason, and alert the owner without silently skipping data.
Retry the poison record forever until the consumer stops failing.
Discard malformed records with no metric to preserve throughput.
Replace the payload with an empty record so parsing succeeds.

feedback.Reason: Error isolation protects good-record progress while retaining evidence for correction.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Streaming consumers can combine retry limits, error topics or S3 sinks, and offsets to make failure visible and replayable.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator tracks error rate and lag, corrects the parser or source, and replays the retained error set after validation.
Details.errorCorrection: A dead-letter path needs its own retention, encryption, access, and capacity controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Isolation improves availability but creates a remediation queue that must have an owner.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unbounded retry blocks progress and can exhaust the retention window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Silent discard loses evidence and makes completeness impossible to assess.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Mutation hides the source error and can create a false business event.

items.prompt: A Kinesis stream carries regulated data and the organization requires a customer-managed KMS key with least-privilege producers and consumers. What should be verified?
constraints: Key policy is separate from IAM.

options.text: Enable server-side encryption with the approved KMS key, grant the service and data-plane roles only required use permissions, and test key disablement and rotation behavior.
Grant all stream users kms:*, including key administration.
Put the key material in each record for consumer convenience.
Rely on VPC isolation instead of encryption at rest.

feedback.Reason: KMS, service, stream, and role policies must all permit the intended encrypted path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis server-side encryption uses KMS for data at rest while IAM and key policies govern access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security owner tests producer put, consumer read, denied admin, key rotation, and recovery access with audit logs.
Details.errorCorrection: A disabled or inaccessible key can make retained data unreadable and needs an operational response.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customer-managed encryption improves control but introduces key availability and policy coupling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Data-plane encryption use does not require broad key administration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Key material must never be embedded in event payloads.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Network isolation does not protect stored stream records or service backups.

items.prompt: An MSK Connect connector needs a database password and the password rotates regularly. Which secret pattern should be used?
constraints: Operators should not edit connector code for rotation.

options.text: Store credentials in Secrets Manager with a scoped access policy, integrate the connector's supported secret mechanism, and test rotation without exposing values in logs or configuration.
Put the password in the connector name and task logs.
Bake the password into a connector image that never changes.
Grant the connector account administrator access to every secret.

feedback.Reason: Managed secret retrieval separates credential rotation from connector code and limits exposure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Secrets Manager stores and rotates sensitive values while IAM and connector configuration govern retrieval.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests initial access, rotation, failure during rotation, and log redaction with the connector task role.
Details.errorCorrection: Connector support for dynamic refresh varies and may require a controlled restart or version change.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Secret integration reduces manual credential handling but adds rotation and availability dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Names and logs are broadly visible and are not secret stores.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Immutable images do not solve rotation and leave credentials exposed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The connector should read only the specific secret and version it needs.

items.prompt: A central account owns a Kinesis stream, while producer accounts should have put-only access and no ability to read or administer it. What should be aligned?
constraints: The stream owner controls encryption and retention.

options.text: Use a cross-account resource and identity policy that permits only required put actions, align KMS permissions, and verify denied read, delete, and administration paths.
Share the stream administrator role with every producer account.
Make the stream public and use the stream name as a credential.
Grant producers read access so they can confirm every event.

feedback.Reason: Cross-account ingestion needs a narrow producer permission path and separate ownership of retention and keys.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis resource policies and IAM or KMS policies can compose cross-account data-plane access according to service support.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests successful put, denied read and delete, key access, and CloudTrail ownership across accounts.
Details.errorCorrection: Service-specific cross-account policy support and regional boundaries must be checked before deployment.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central ownership simplifies governance but requires explicit trust and key-policy coordination.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Administrative sharing violates the put-only boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A resource name is not authorization and public access exposes data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Read access is outside the producer contract and can expose other tenants' records.

items.prompt: A security team needs evidence of who changed a stream, delivery stream, connector, or encryption configuration. What should record the control-plane actions?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail organization or account trails for the relevant service APIs, protect the log destination, and alert on unauthorized or high-risk configuration changes.
Record only application event payloads.
Let each operator keep a local change note instead of API logs.
Allow the logging bucket to be deleted by the stream administrator.

feedback.Reason: Control-plane audit connects configuration changes to AWS principals and time.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudTrail records supported AWS API activity and can deliver protected evidence to a separate logging boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security owner tests an authorized change, denied change, log delivery, retention, and alert routing.
Details.errorCorrection: CloudTrail data-event and service coverage differ, so the exact required event types need validation.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Protected audit logs add storage and review cost but support incident reconstruction.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Payloads do not prove which principal changed service configuration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Manual notes are incomplete and cannot establish actual API activity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The subject being audited should not be able to erase the audit trail unilaterally.

items.prompt: A streaming pipeline has no alert until records expire from retention, even though consumer lag grows for hours. Which signals should drive early action?
constraints: Consumer lag and age are measurable.
Capacity can be changed or input shaped.

options.text: Alert on backlog age, iterator or consumer lag, incoming and outgoing rate, throttling, error rate, delivery failures, and remaining retention headroom.
Alert only when the stream is deleted.
Monitor CPU on the producer and ignore consumer lag.
Reset offsets without investigating the backlog.

feedback.Reason: Lag and age connect the processing bottleneck to the time remaining for recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis and Kafka expose consumer lag, throughput, throttling, and retention-related metrics for operational control.
Details.scenarioApplication: The on-call runbook scales consumers or partitions, throttles producers, preserves error records, and escalates before expiry.
Details.errorCorrection: A low lag count can still be dangerous when record age is high or event rate is changing.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Early alerts create response work but avoid silent data loss and emergency recovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Deletion is far too late to protect data or recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Producer CPU does not reveal a downstream backlog or retention risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Offset changes can skip or replay data without fixing capacity or correctness.

items.prompt: Multiple producers send JSON events to a shared stream and one producer begins sending an incompatible field type. What should happen at the ingestion boundary?

options.text: Validate and version the event schema at the producer or ingestion boundary, reject or quarantine incompatible records with reasons, and preserve valid events without silently coercing meaning.
Accept every payload and let each consumer guess the type.
Drop the entire stream until every producer is upgraded.
Convert every value to a string regardless of its business meaning.

feedback.Reason: Schema enforcement prevents one producer change from silently breaking every consumer.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Ingestion services transport records but schema registry or validation logic defines application compatibility.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner records schema version, routes invalid records to a protected error path, and coordinates producer rollout.
Details.errorCorrection: Schema validation adds CPU and operational ownership and must support legitimate evolution.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strict contracts improve reliability but require a clear versioning and migration process.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Consumer-specific guessing creates inconsistent semantics and hidden failures.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A single producer error should be isolated when the contract supports partial recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Lossy coercion can make invalid values appear valid and corrupt calculations.

items.prompt: A workload has 2 KB records, a burst rate four times its average, and three independent consumers. What should capacity planning include?
constraints: Record size and burst rate are known.

options.text: Model producer bytes and records, partition-key distribution, consumer read throughput per group or registered consumer, retention, downstream capacity, and burst headroom.
Size only for average records per second and ignore the burst.
Size only producer writes because consumers share unlimited read capacity.
Use the number of applications as the only partition count.

feedback.Reason: End-to-end throughput is constrained by the producer, stream partitions, consumers, and sinks.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis and Kafka capacity models expose record or byte throughput and partition or consumer boundaries.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect replays burst distributions, measures lag and throttling, and reserves capacity for retries and replay.
Details.errorCorrection: Averages and nominal service limits are not substitutes for a representative workload test.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Headroom costs money but protects freshness and recovery under the stated burst.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Average rate can hide throttling and backlog during the required burst.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Consumer read limits and downstream processing are separate capacity dimensions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Partitions depend on rate, size, ordering, and key distribution rather than application count alone.

items.prompt: A regional ingestion service feeds a disaster-recovery Region, but the business requires no silent loss and accepts replay after failover. What should be designed?
constraints: The business needs an explicit RPO and RTO.

options.text: Define the regional failure RPO and RTO, replicate or dual-publish where justified, retain source events durably, and rehearse consumer restart and replay in the recovery Region.
Assume a regional stream is automatically available in every Region.
Delete source events after the primary consumer acknowledges them.
Fail over by changing DNS with no offset or duplicate plan.

feedback.Reason: Multi-Region ingestion requires a data-copy, offset, replay, and cutover contract in addition to endpoint routing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis, MSK, and Firehose have service-specific replication and destination patterns that must be designed explicitly.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests a Region outage, identifies the last durable event, replays safely, and reconciles duplicates and gaps after recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Dual publishing can create duplicates and cost and must be paired with event identity and idempotent sinks.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher resilience adds transfer, storage, and operational complexity but may be required by the RPO.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Regional service resources and retention do not automatically provide cross-Region recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Source retention may be needed to rebuild or reconcile the recovery path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS does not establish replicated data or safe consumer position.

items.prompt: A public ingestion API accepts records from mobile clients with variable payload sizes and one client begins sending oversized or deeply nested events. What boundary should protect the stream?
constraints: Payload size and schema are bounded.

options.text: Enforce request size, schema, nesting, and rate limits at the front door, reject invalid records with an actionable status, and keep accepted events on the durable path.
Accept any payload and let consumers fail later.
Increase stream capacity to handle malformed payloads.
Truncate oversized records silently.

feedback.Reason: Input validation prevents malformed or abusive payloads from becoming a downstream capacity and correctness incident.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: API Gateway request validation, throttling, and integration limits can protect a durable streaming destination.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures rejected size and schema rates, returns explicit errors, and preserves accepted event identity for retries.
Details.errorCorrection: Limits need to match the downstream service's record and batch limits and should be tested at the maximum supported size.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strict validation may require client rollout but protects the shared ingestion boundary.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Late failure consumes capacity and makes the producer contract ambiguous.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Capacity does not correct invalid input or protect downstream memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Silent truncation changes business data and can make a valid-looking but incorrect event.

items.prompt: A new tenant will triple event volume and the current design is close to regional service quotas. What should be done before launch?
constraints: Service quotas and limits can change by Region.

options.text: Model producer, partition, consumer, connector, endpoint, and account quotas, request increases where appropriate, and load-test the forecast with operational headroom.
Launch first and request increases only after throttling begins.
Assume every managed service scales without quotas.
Remove monitoring so quota alarms do not block the launch.

feedback.Reason: Capacity planning includes service quotas and failure behavior, not only average throughput.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS Service Quotas and service documentation expose adjustable and fixed limits for many ingestion components.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform tests the forecast, records approved quota increases, and alarms on usage percentage before the tenant is enabled.
Details.errorCorrection: Some limits are hard or partition-specific and require workload redesign instead of a quota request.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Headroom has a cost but is cheaper than a launch-time throttling and recovery event.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Quota requests and propagation can take longer than the launch incident window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Managed services still expose account, partition, API, and regional limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Hiding quota signals increases the chance of silent lag or loss.
